newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl reassures residents in flood-hit Germany.
newsitem.headline: Kohl reassures residents in flood-hit Germany.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl arrived in flood-hit eastern Germany on Tuesday, interrupting his summer holiday to offer encouragement to residents, relief workers and soldiers.

Kohl told residents in the town of Bad Freienwalde that defending the area was a task for the whole nation and demonstrated the solidarity between west and east Germans, seven years after the unification of the country.
"The main thing I want to say, in this first natural disaster seven years after unification, is that we not only express ourselves in words but also in deeds," he said.
"We want to ensure that people here feel our compassion in a special way. This is a national task."

Kohl, who flew in from his Austrian vacation resort dressed in a casual suede jacket, said the federal and state governments were already thinking about how best to repair the dikes on the Oder river before the annual high water arrived in autumn.

A team of 700 soldiers and relief workers battled overnight to shore up a six- to seven-metre (yard) section of one dike, which had collapsed and nearly caused a total break in the dam on the Oder River near the village of Hohenwutzen.

Kohl, paying his second visit to the region, said the government planned to let the army stay throughout the summer to ensure repairs were completed by the autumn. He said it might be time to erect more modern flood protection along the river.
"We have to think about whether these dams, which are 250 years old, should be kept in this form," said the chancellor, who was greeted with applause by local people on his arrival.
"No one should fear we will give up any of these areas," he said. "The army plans to stay to defend the dikes."

Kohl said people whose property had been damaged by flood waters needed quick and high-quality help. "I will personally ensure that the large insurance companies quickly determine the extent of damage," he pledged.
Matthias Platzeck, the environment minister for Brandenburg, the German state worst affected by the floods, said he was considering shoring up more of the dike at Hohenwutzen.
"That appears to be the most vulnerable section, although exact predictions after 12 or 13 days of continuous (water) pressure are no longer possible," he said.
"We've had the greatest pressure on these dikes for all this time and it's pressure which is far above what they were designed for," Platzeck told ZDF television.
At Ratzdorf, where the Oder and Neisse rivers meet, relief workers had begun building up an 800-metre (-yard) secondary dike, anticipating a possible break in the main dam near the town.
Brandenburg officials said a new wave of high water was approaching Ratzdorf and would reach the most critical areas of the east German stretch of the Oder later in the day.
The floods have claimed more than 100 lives in neighbouring Poland and the Czech Republic.

Germany has so far escaped the worst of the damage. But thousands of people have already been evacuated from their homes and thousands more are on standby to leave at a moment's notice if the dikes give way.

Officials said up to nine helicopters had flown non-stop during the overnight operation, which was continuing by day. Around 100,000 sandbags had been used to plug the gap and another 100,000 had been ordered, Platzeck said.
He said the operation to construct a second line of defence by raising up old dikes was a precaution and he was hopeful they would limit flooding if the first dike burst.
"The condition (of the old dikes) is relatively good, although they haven't been used for decades, or even centuries in some cases," he said.
"Nevertheless, we want to do the maximum to hold the first line of defence because there's a lot of places in front of the secondary dikes and they should stay as dry as possible."
